title: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
wiki_lead:
The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (IPA: [dʒəlɪjãːʋaːlaː baːɣ, baːɡ]), also known as the Amritsar massacre, took place on 13 April 1919. A large crowd had gathered at the Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, Punjab, British India, during the annual Baisakhi fair to protest against the Rowlatt Act and the arrest of pro-Indian independence activists Saifuddin Kitchlew and Satyapal. In response to the public gathering, Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer surrounded the people with Gurkhas of Nepalese origin and Sikh infantrymen of the British Indian Army.
The Jallianwala Bagh could only be exited on one side, as its other three sides were enclosed by buildings. After blocking the exit with his troops, Dyer ordered them to shoot at the crowd, continuing to fire even as the protestors tried to flee. The troops kept on firing until their ammunition was low and they were ordered to stop. Estimates of those killed vary from 379 to 1,500 or more people; over 1,200 others were injured, of whom 192 sustained serious injury. Britain has never formally apologised for the massacre, but expressed deep "regret" in 2019.
The massacre caused a re-evaluation by the Imperial British military of its role when confronted with civilians to use "minimal force whenever possible" (although the British Army was not directly involved in the massacre; the British Indian Army was a separate organisation). However, in the light of later British military actions during the Mau Mau rebellion in the Kenya Colony, historian Huw Bennett has pointed out that this new policy was not always followed. The army was retrained with less violent tactics for crowd control.
The level of casual brutality and the lack of any accountability stunned the entire nation, resulting in a wrenching loss of faith of the general Indian public in the intentions of the United Kingdom. The attack was condemned by the Secretary of State for War, Winston Churchill, as "unutterably monstrous", and in the UK House of Commons debate on 8 July 1920 Members of Parliament voted 247 to 37 against Dyer. The ineffective inquiry, together with the initial accolades for Dyer, fuelled great widespread anger against the British among the Indian populace, leading to the non-cooperation movement of 1920–22.

Background


Defence of India Act

During World War I, British India contributed to the British war effort by providing men and resources. Millions of Indian soldiers and labourers served in Europe, Africa, and the Middle East, while both the Indian administration and the princes sent large supplies of food, money, and ammunition. Bengal and Punjab remained sources of anti-colonial activities. Revolutionary attacks in Bengal, associated increasingly with disturbances in Punjab, were enough to nearly paralyse the regional administration. grok_lead: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on 13 April 1919, when approximately 50 British Indian Army troops under Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer fired without prior warning into a crowd of several thousand unarmed Indian civilians assembled in the enclosed Jallianwala Bagh public garden in Amritsar, Punjab province of British India, killing at least 379 people and wounding over 1,100 according to the official British Hunter Commission inquiry, though contemporaneous Indian estimates claimed more than 1,000 deaths. The gathering, which included pilgrims observing the Baisakhi harvest festival and protesters defying a recent ban on public assemblies amid opposition to the Rowlatt Act's repressive provisions, occurred in a walled space with limited exits, where troops discharged about 1,650 rounds over roughly ten minutes until their ammunition supply dwindled. Dyer later testified that the action aimed to produce a "moral effect" and restore order following days of local anti-British violence, including the mob killing of five Europeans on 10 April and an assault on British missionary woman Miss Sherwood, which had prompted martial law declarations and measures like the enforced "crawling order" on affected streets. The preceding unrest in Amritsar stemmed from arrests of local leaders protesting the Rowlatt Act âwhich empowered indefinite detention without trialâand escalated into riots targeting British banks, post offices, and residents, fueling British fears of a widespread revolt reminiscent of the 1857 Indian uprising. Dyer, assuming temporary command after arriving in the city, viewed the Jallianwala Bagh assembly as a direct challenge to authority that required exemplary force to avert further chaos, blocking the main exit during the firing and later justifying the lack of warning or cease-fire as essential to maximize deterrence. The Hunter Commission, appointed by the British government to investigate, condemned the episode as disproportionate and lacking proportionality, censuring Dyer for failing to minimize casualties and recommending his removal from duty, a view echoed in Winston Churchill's parliamentary description of the event as "monstrous" and without precedent in British military annals. In India, the massacre intensified nationalist outrage, galvanizing non-cooperation movements led by Mohandas Gandhi and marking a causal turning point toward mass civil disobedience against colonial rule, though it also highlighted tensions between peaceful satyagraha ideals and localized mob violence that British officials cited as precipitating factors. Controversies endure over casualty discrepanciesâofficial figures derived from hospital records and identifications versus unsubstantiated higher claims in nationalist accountsâand the episode's framing, with some contemporary British supporters defending Dyer's decisiveness amid post-World War I imperial anxieties, while later historiographies, often influenced by anti-colonial perspectives in academic institutions, emphasize unprovoked brutality over the riotous context. The site today preserves bullet-scarred walls and a martyrs' well into which victims reportedly jumped for cover, serving as a memorial to the dead and a locus of reflection on colonial governance's use of lethal force.
